readerTitle: Why In-N-Out never added the chicken sandwich
caseNote: 실제 기업 (In-N-Out Burger, McDonald's) + 가상 적용 (버거 체인 의사결정 장면, 일정관리 소프트웨어)
insight: 메뉴 항목 하나의 비용은 그 항목을 주문한 손님만이 아니라 모든 주문이 나눠 낸다. 다양성은 재료와 공정을 공유할 때만 흐름을 깨지 않는다.
misconception: 메뉴나 옵션을 늘리면 더 많은 손님을 잡을 수 있고, 새 항목의 비용은 그 항목을 파는 만큼만 든다.

factChecks.note: In-N-Out 창업 연도(1948), 창업자(Harry & Esther Snyder), 첫 매장 위치(캘리포니아 Baldwin Park)를 공식 사이트 History 페이지에서 다시 확인하세요.
'냉동고, 보온램프, 전자레인지가 없다'와 '감자를 매장에서 직접 썬다'는 회사의 공식 주장입니다. 공식 사이트 문구로 재확인하고, 카드에는 'the company says'로 회사 주장임을 밝혔습니다.
'핵심 메뉴가 수십 년간 거의 바뀌지 않았다'는 널리 보도된 내용이지만 음료·소소한 항목 추가 이력이 있을 수 있습니다. 카드에는 'has changed little'로만 적었습니다. 구체적인 메뉴 항목 수는 쓰지 않았습니다.
McDonald's: 2010년대 메뉴 확대와 서비스 지연 문제, 2015년 메뉴 간소화 발표, 2020년 드라이브스루 속도를 위한 메뉴 축소를 당시 보도로 확인하세요. 구체적인 항목 수나 대기 시간 수치는 확인되지 않아 쓰지 않았습니다.
짧은 메뉴와 In-N-Out의 성공 사이의 인과관계는 단정할 수 없습니다. 가족 소유, 느린 확장, 직원 처우 등 다른 요인도 있어 7번 카드에서 한계로 다뤘습니다.

cards.title: Why In-N-Out never added the chicken sandwich
body: Fast-food chains keep adding things: wraps, salads, breakfast, limited-time specials. The logic seems obvious. More choice brings in more customers.
In-N-Out Burger went the other way. Its core menu is burgers, fries, shakes and drinks, and it has changed little in decades. The lines are still out the door.

image.label: A short burger menu board next to a long one
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 항목이 4줄뿐인 짧은 메뉴판, 오른쪽에 빽빽하게 넘쳐나는 긴 메뉴판. 짧은 메뉴판 앞에는 빠르게 움직이는 줄, 긴 메뉴판 앞에는 멈춘 줄. 실제 브랜드 로고, 색상 배치, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rivals are adding items. Do you?
body: You run a growing chain of burger stands. Rivals are adding chicken, salads and breakfast. Some families tell you they skip your place because one of them doesn't want a burger.

options.text: Add chicken, salads and breakfast to match rivals
options.feedback: You may win some families. But every new item needs its own ingredients, steps and training, and that slows the line for every customer who came for a burger.

options.text: Keep the short menu and put the effort into speed and freshness
options.feedback: You give up some customers on purpose. In return, each order follows the same few steps, so the kitchen stays fast and the few items stay excellent.

options.text: Add just one item, a chicken sandwich
options.feedback: One item sounds small, but it often needs a new fryer, a new ingredient and a new station. The question is not how much it sells but what it does to everything else.

cards.title: In-N-Out chose the short menu, and built around it.
body: Harry and Esther Snyder opened the first In-N-Out in 1948 in Baldwin Park, California. The family-owned chain has kept its menu short ever since.

Because the menu is short, the kitchen can work in ways most chains can't. The company says its restaurants have no freezers, heat lamps or microwaves. Beef arrives fresh, and fries are cut from whole potatoes in each store.
A long menu would make that impossible. Too many ingredients would need to be stored, prepared and kept ready.

cards.title: Complexity cost
body: **Complexity cost** is the hidden price of variety. Each extra item adds ingredients, steps, equipment and decisions. That cost is not paid only by people who order the item. It's paid by every order, because the whole kitchen gets slower and harder to run.
A short menu protects **flow**: work moving through the same few steps without stopping, switching or waiting. When every order looks alike, staff get fast and mistakes get rare.

image.label: One smooth line of orders versus tangled paths
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 위쪽: 주문 티켓들이 3개 스테이션(Grill → Assemble → Serve)을 일직선으로 매끄럽게 통과. 아래쪽: 같은 티켓들이 Fryer, Salad, Breakfast 등 여러 스테이션 사이를 엉킨 화살표로 오가며 중간중간 멈춤 표시. 로고 없음.

cards.title: McDonald's learned it the hard way.
body: Through the 2000s and early 2010s, McDonald's kept adding items. The menu grew long, and the company and its franchise owners said the variety was slowing kitchens and drive-thrus.
In 2015, McDonald's began trimming its menu. In 2020, it cut items again to speed up service. The goal both times was the same: fewer things to make, so each order moves faster.
cards.callout: Adding items was easy. Taking them back out took years.

cards.title: Variety without new steps.
body: In-N-Out does offer choice. It just builds it from the same ingredients. Its well-known "not-so-secret menu" includes:
list: **Animal Style:** the same burger with extra spread, pickles and grilled onions
**Protein Style:** lettuce instead of a bun
cards.callout: Customers get thousands of combinations. The kitchen still does the same few things.
cards.softwareNote: The same idea appears in software as settings versus forks. Options built from shared parts are cheap. A separate version for one customer must be built, tested and supported on its own forever.

cards.title: A short menu is not a free win.
body: It only works when customers come for the core item and that item is excellent. A short menu of average food is just less food.
You also lose people on purpose, like the group with one non-burger eater. In-N-Out accepts that cost.
And be careful with the lesson. In-N-Out is also family-owned, grows slowly and is known for treating staff well. The short menu is one part of a larger system, not the whole reason it works.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Your team of eight builds a scheduling app and ships updates every week. Three large clients each ask for their own custom version, with different screens and rules. Together they'd add a lot of revenue.

options.feedback: You win the revenue now. But every future update must be built and tested four times, and weekly releases slow down for every user.

options.text: Keep one product and add a few settings built from existing parts
options.feedback: Like Animal Style, clients get variety without new steps. You may lose a client who wants something truly different, but your team keeps its speed.

options.text: Build a custom version only for the biggest client
options.feedback: Less damage than three, but one fork still doubles your testing and support. Check if a setting could meet the same need first.

cards.title: Every option you add is paid for by every customer.
body: Before adding an item, a service or a feature, ask what it does to the steps everyone else goes through. The best variety reuses what you already make.
**Try it today:** list everything you sell. Mark each item that needs its own ingredient, tool or step. Which ones earn that cost?
